chapters.title: Chapter 4: Currencies, Commodities and Managing Risk

lessons.title: Currency Markets: How Rupee Moves Hit Imports, Exports and Overseas Costs

children.text: The currency market is the largest market in the world and the one most people misread. A four rupee move in the dollar rate sounds like a rounding error and can wipe out a quarter's margin, or hand a company a windfall nobody in sales earned. This lesson covers how to read a quote, who gains and loses, and where currency reaches your own salary.
Reading the Quote Without Getting It Backwards

markDefs.definition: The price of one currency in terms of another. In India, the dollar rate is quoted as the number of rupees needed to buy one US dollar.
A fall in the value of a currency, meaning more rupees are needed to buy the same dollar. Also loosely called the rupee weakening.
The rate for immediate delivery, as against a forward rate agreed today for settlement on a future date.

children.text: The
exchange rate

for the dollar is quoted as rupees per dollar, so ₹83 means one dollar costs 83 rupees. When that number moves from 83 to 87, the rupee has not gone up. It has weakened, because you now need more rupees for the same dollar. That is
depreciation
. The rate quoted for immediate transactions is the
spot rate
, and a rate agreed today for a payment months away is a forward rate, which the next two lessons build on.

body.text: A rising number means a falling rupee. Headlines that say "rupee hits a new high of 87" have it wrong: 87 is a new low for the rupee and a new high for the dollar. Get this one direction right and you will understand currency news better than most people in the room.

body.caption: Measured in rupees per dollar, a rise in the rate is a fall in the rupee.

body.title: Size the Move
body.prompt: The rupee moves from ₹83 to ₹87 per US dollar. By what percentage has it depreciated? Give your answer in %.
body.explanation: (87 − 83) ÷ 83 × 100 = about 4.82%. Under 5% sounds mild, but applied to a company importing USD 20 million a year it is roughly ₹8 crore of extra cost, with nothing else in the business having changed.

points: IT services and pharma exporters billing in dollars

Employees paid in foreign currency but spending in rupees

children.text: Run the numbers on both sides and the scale becomes clear. Take one exporter billing USD 5 million a quarter and one importer buying USD 2 million of components a quarter.

body.text: Currency moves transfer money between companies without any change in how well those companies are run. Treating a currency windfall as operational brilliance, or a currency loss as a failure of the team, is one of the most common mistakes in corporate reviews.

body.title: Who Is Smiling?
body.question: The rupee weakens sharply against the dollar over one quarter. Whose margins are most likely to improve, with everything else unchanged?
options: A Bengaluru IT services firm earning 80% of revenue in dollars with costs in rupees
A Chennai electronics assembler importing most of its components
An airline buying jet fuel priced off dollar-denominated crude
An Indian company repaying a dollar loan taken three years ago
body.explanation: The IT firm earns in dollars and pays salaries, its largest cost, in rupees, so a weaker rupee converts the same dollar revenue into more rupees while costs barely move. The other three are all paying out in dollars or in dollar-linked prices, so their costs rise.

body.title: An Illustrative Rupee Path Across Six Quarters

children.text: Notice the shape. The rupee tends to drift weaker in small steps over long periods, punctuated by sharp falls in stressed months. A budget built on last year's average rate is therefore wrong by default, and usually wrong in the costlier direction for importers.

events.title: Devaluation Amid a Crisis
events.description: Facing a balance of payments crisis and dwindling reserves, India devalued the rupee in two sharp steps, which became the trigger for wider economic reform.

events.title: From Fixed to Market-Determined
events.description: India moved through a transitional dual rate system to a largely market-determined exchange rate, with RBI intervening to smooth volatility rather than to fix the level.

events.title: The Taper Shock
events.description: When the US signalled it would slow its bond buying, capital rushed out of emerging markets and the rupee fell sharply within weeks, a reminder that global decisions move the rupee more than domestic news often does.

events.title: Pandemic Volatility
events.description: Global risk aversion, collapsing trade and extraordinary monetary policy abroad made currency markets unusually turbulent.

events.title: A Strong Dollar Era
events.description: Aggressive US rate hikes strengthened the dollar against almost every currency, and the rupee crossed levels previously considered unthinkable, while RBI used its reserves to slow the descent.

children.text: Six forces do most of the work, and only two of them are domestic:
The trade balance.
India imports more than it exports, so there is persistent demand for dollars to pay for those imports, which is a structural weight on the rupee.
Crude oil.
Oil is India's largest import and is priced in dollars, so a rising crude price increases dollar demand and pressures the rupee at the same time as it raises costs at home.
Foreign capital flows.
Foreign investors buying Indian shares and bonds must first buy rupees, which supports the currency. When they sell and leave, the reverse happens fast.
Interest rate differentials.
When US rates rise, dollar deposits become more attractive relative to rupee assets, pulling capital away and weakening the rupee. This is the link back to Chapter 3.
Inflation differences.
Over long periods, a currency with higher inflation tends to lose value against one with lower inflation, which is the main reason the rupee trends weaker decade after decade.
RBI intervention.
RBI buys and sells dollars from its reserves to smooth sharp moves. It does not fix the rate, and it cannot indefinitely defend a level the fundamentals do not support.

body.label: Nobody Sets the Rupee
body.context: The rate comes from trading between banks, importers, exporters and investors. RBI manages volatility using its foreign exchange reserves, but the level itself is not announced or fixed by anyone.

body.text: Individuals sending money abroad, whether for education, travel, property or foreign shares, do so under an annual per-person limit prescribed under RBI's liberalised remittance framework. If your role involves advising employees on overseas assignments or education support, confirm the current limit and the applicable tax collection at source before quoting figures.

body.title: The Onsite Allowance That Stopped Working
body.scenario: You are an HR manager at a Pune IT services company. Six engineers were deputed to a client site in the United States on a fixed monthly allowance of ₹2,60,000, converted locally at whatever rate applies. When the policy was set, the rupee was around ₹83 to the dollar, giving them roughly USD 3,130 a month. The rupee is now near ₹87, so the same allowance converts to about USD 2,990. Two engineers have written in saying they are struggling with rent and asking for a revision.
body.prompt: What has actually gone wrong in the policy design, and what would you recommend?
body.modelAnswer: The design error is that the allowance is denominated in the wrong currency. The engineers' costs are in dollars, since rent, groceries and transport are all paid locally, but the allowance is fixed in rupees, so every rupee depreciation quietly cuts their real purchasing power. At ₹83 they received about USD 3,130; at ₹87 the same ₹2,60,000 converts to about USD 2,990, a cut of roughly USD 140 a month that nobody decided to make. Their complaint is legitimate and arithmetic, not a negotiation tactic. The clean fix is to denominate onsite allowances in the currency where the money is spent, so the policy states USD 3,130 a month and the company bears the rupee cost of delivering it, which is the correct place for that risk to sit, since the company can hedge and an individual employee cannot. If a rupee-denominated structure must be retained for payroll reasons, then add a stated review trigger, such as an automatic revision whenever the rate moves more than 3%, so the correction is systematic rather than dependent on employees complaining. Two supporting recommendations: ask finance whether the underlying client contract is billed in dollars, because if it is, the company is receiving more rupees from the same contract while paying deputed staff less in real terms, which is difficult to defend; and for future deputations, document the assumed exchange rate in the offer letter so nobody is surprised later. Finally, apply the revision to all six engineers, not only the two who wrote in.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: When the rupee moves from ₹83 to ₹87 per US dollar, the rupee has undergone ___ against the dollar.
body.explanation: More rupees are now needed for the same dollar, so the rupee has depreciated. The dollar has appreciated by the mirror image of that move.

body.title: Find Your Company's Currency Exposure
steps: List every inflow and outflow that is in a foreign currency, including cloud services, software licences and overseas advertising, which are easy to forget
Check whether inflows and outflows are in the same currency, since a natural offset reduces the risk before any hedging is needed
Find the exchange rate assumed in this year's budget, and compare it with today's rate
Ask which currency your contracts are denominated in, because that single clause decides who carries the risk
Check whether foreign currency borrowings are hedged, since an unhedged dollar loan is a currency bet on top of a borrowing decision
Confirm who in the company is allowed to take a hedging decision, and whether a written policy exists

body.label: RBI: Exchange Rates and Reference Rates
body.description: RBI publishes reference rates for major currencies along with data on foreign exchange reserves and trade. Useful when you need an official rate for a budget assumption rather than a number from a news ticker.

points: The dollar rate is quoted in rupees per dollar, so a rising number means a weakening rupee
A move from ₹83 to ₹87 is about 4.8%, which on USD 20 million of annual imports is roughly ₹8 crore of extra cost
The same move helps exporters and employees earning in foreign currency, and hurts importers, foreign currency borrowers, travellers and students abroad
Currency gains and losses are not management performance, so treating them as such distorts reviews and incentives
The rupee is driven mainly by the trade balance, crude prices, foreign capital flows, interest rate differentials and inflation differences, with RBI smoothing volatility rather than fixing the level
Long-run inflation differences explain why the rupee trends weaker over decades, so budgets should not assume a stable rate
Allowances, tuition support and overseas contracts should be denominated in the currency where the money is actually spent

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial, tax or investment advice. All exchange rates, company figures and rate paths used are illustrative teaching examples, not current market levels or forecasts. Remittance limits, tax collection at source and foreign exchange rules are set by RBI and the tax authorities and change over time, so verify the current position before acting.
